short.headline: 145.1 crore and slowing fast
short.dek: India’s population tripled since 1960, but annual growth has fallen to 0.9% as fertility dips below two births per woman.
short.body: In 2024, India had an estimated 145.1 crore people, up from 43.6 crore in 1960. The growth rate has declined from 2.4% in 1961 to 0.9% in 2024. Fertility fell from 5.92 births per woman in 1960 to 1.96 in 2024. The population pyramid shows a large working-age bulge and a narrowing base. Median age is rising, and dependency ratios are shifting from children to older adults. Future scenarios range from 99.1 crore to 219.7 crore by 2100, depending on fertility assumptions.

macha.heading: Okay, but what does this actually mean, macha?
macha.body: India now has 145.1 crore people. That is a huge number, but the big story is that growth has slowed from a sprint to a walk. Fewer babies are being born, and we are living longer. The country is still young, but it is aging fast. For a few more decades, there will be a lot of working-age folks and fewer children to support. The tricky part: the old-age dependency is going to rise, and we need to plan for that now. The data does not tell us if that is good or bad; it says get ready.
macha.soWhat: India’s population is still growing, but the wheels are slowing — and the age structure is shifting from pyramid to pillar.

article.title: India's population: 145.1 crore and growing slower
article.standfirst: India's population reached 145.1 crore in 2024, tripling since 1960. Growth has slowed sharply to 0.9% as fertility dips below two births per woman. This data unpack explores the age structure, dependency burdens, and future scenarios.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## What is India’s population today, and how much has it grown since 1960?

India’s population in 2024 is an estimated 145.1 crore, according to the World Bank. That is more than three times the 43.6 crore people counted in 1960. The line chart above plots this journey: a steady climb that steepens after 1980 before starting to level off in recent years.

A population estimate is not a live count. It is pieced together from censuses, surveys, and records of births and deaths. The actual number can never be known with complete certainty, but this is the best available figure.

## Who are these 145.1 crore people? What does the age and sex structure look like in 2025?

Using a UN median projection for 2030 as the closest available snapshot, the age-sex structure reveals a large working-age bulge. The largest five-year group is 20-24, with 12.5 crore people. The pyramid is narrowing at the base: only 11.1 crore children under five, indicating that smaller cohorts are replacing larger ones.

A population pyramid splits the population by age and sex. The left side shows males, the right females. When the pyramid has a wide middle and a narrower base, it means a country has passed its high-fertility years and is starting to age.

## How fast is India’s population still growing each year?

The annual growth rate peaked at 2.4% in 1961 and has fallen steadily to 0.9% in 2024. Even that 0.9% adds about 1.3 crore people each year because the base is so large. A declining growth rate does not mean the population is shrinking. It means it is expanding more slowly.

## Why is the growth rate slowing? What has happened to the number of births per woman?

One visible reason in this data is the fertility decline. In 1960, the average Indian woman could expect to have 5.92 children over her lifetime. By 2024, that had fallen to 1.96. A rate below 2.1, the so-called replacement level, means each generation will be smaller than the one before. Fewer births, even as life expectancy rises, are curbing the growth rate. Fertility is just one driver; mortality and migration also matter, but the drop is the headline force.

## What share of the population are children, working-age adults, and older people?

In 2024, 24.6% of India's population was under 15, down from 40.6% in 1960. The working-age share (15–64) has risen from 56.1% to 68.2%. The older population (65+) has more than doubled its share, from 3.3% to 7.1%. This shift is the demographic dividend: a larger share of people in their productive years, with fewer children to support.

## How old is the typical Indian? What is the median age, and where is it headed?

India’s median age is rising. In 2000, it was 21.19 years. By 2100, under the UN’s median scenario, it could reach 47.78 years. That means half the population will be older than 48. A higher median age signals an aging society, but it does not mean there are no young people. It reflects the shift from high to low birth rates.

## How has India’s age mix shifted over the decades?

The three lines on the chart tell the story. The share of children (0–14) has fallen from 40.6% in 1960 to 24.6% in 2024. The working-age share (15–64) rose from 56.1% to 68.2%. The older share (65+) is still small but growing, from 3.3% to 7.1%. This is the demographic transition: as fewer children are born and adults live longer, the population ages. The window when the working-age share is at its peak is a one-time opportunity.

## How long can an Indian newborn expect to live today?

In 2000, life expectancy at birth was 62.75 years. By 2030, it is projected to reach 73.63 years. Women outlive men by about 3.4 years: 75.41 for females against 71.99 for males. Life expectancy at birth is a summary of current death rates, not a prophecy for anyone alive today. It says: if mortality patterns stayed the same, a newborn would live this long on average.

## Once someone reaches age 60, how many more years can they expect?

In 2021, a 60‑year‑old woman could expect about 16.51 more years, while a man could expect 14.76 years. Life expectancy at 60 had been improving: in 2020, the combined figure was 17.8 years. The drop to 15.62 years in 2021 reflects the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. These numbers are averages; many people live longer, and some shorter.

## What are the chances of a child dying before age five or before their first birthday?

In 2023, 27.75 out of every 1,000 children born alive died before their fifth birthday. Of those, most died before turning one: the infant mortality rate was 24.5 per 1,000. The gap between these two rates shows that the highest risk is concentrated in the first year of life. Both rates have fallen sharply from previous decades, but they remain a reminder of uneven access to healthcare.

## How many children does each 100 working-age adults have to support?

The child dependency ratio measures how many children aged 0–14 there are for every 100 people of working age (15–64). In 2030, under the median scenario, that ratio is 32.4. In 2000, it was 59.22. A lower ratio means fewer children per potential earner. Not every adult works, and not every child is dependent, but the measure tracks broad demographic pressure.

## And how many older adults does each 100 working-age adults support?

The old-age dependency ratio (65+ per 100 aged 15–64) was 7.35 in 2000. By 2030, it is projected to reach 12.4. It will keep climbing as the large working-age generation ages and fertility stays low. A rising ratio does not mean every older person is dependent; many work or have savings. But it signals a growing need for care, pensions, and health services.

## Where is India’s population headed by 2100? What do the scenarios tell us?

Under the UN’s median projection, India’s population will peak around 150.5 crore by 2100. The possible range is enormous. If fertility stays higher, it could reach 219.7 crore. If it drops further, it could fall to 99.1 crore. These scenarios are not predictions. They are ‘what-if’ exercises that show how sensitive the future is to small differences in how many children women have today.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A count of all people living in a country at a given time, pieced together from censuses, surveys, and birth and death records. It is not a real-time count; it is the best available figure.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The 145.1 crore figure is an estimate; the exact number is never known with certainty.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The average number of children a woman would have if she experienced current age-specific birth rates throughout her childbearing years. Think of it as the average family size in a particular year.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Fertility falling below 2 means, on average, each generation is smaller than the one before—this is the main brake on population growth.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The age that splits a population into two equal halves: half are younger, half are older. It is like the middle person in a queue sorted by age.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India’s median age is still young but rising fast as births slow.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The number of people aged 0-14 (child dependency) or 65+ (old-age dependency) per 100 people aged 15-64. It gives a rough measure of how many dependents the working-age population supports.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: A falling child dependency ratio and a still-low old-age dependency ratio is the 'demographic dividend' window when fewer dependents can free up resources.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The average number of years a newborn would live if the death rates at each age stayed the same throughout its life. It reflects today’s health conditions, not a prophecy.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Rising life expectancy means people are living longer, which is good but also increases the number of older people.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The number of babies who die before their first birthday, per 1,000 live births in a given year. It is a sensitive indicator of healthcare quality.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Infant mortality has fallen sharply, but about 24 out of every 1,000 babies still do not reach age one.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A calculation of what could happen in the future if certain trends continue. It is a 'what-if' exercise, not a forecast. Scenarios use different assumptions (e.g., high, medium, low fertility).
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The wide range of population scenarios for 2100 shows how sensitive the future is to how many children women have today.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A rate that counts events (like deaths) relative to every 1,000 babies born alive. It standardizes the risk so you can compare across time or places.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Mortality rates are expressed per 1,000 to make them easier to grasp than very small decimals.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The percentage by which the total population changes from one year to the next. It is the net result of births, deaths, and migration.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: A growth rate of 0.9% still means India added about 1.3 crore people in 2024.

chartExplainers.title: India's population, 1960 to today
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's population reached 145.1 crore in 2024, more than tripling from 43.6 crore in 1960.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart shows the total population of India each year from 1960 to 2024. The count starts at 43.6 crore and rises steadily, steepening in the 1980s and 1990s before the curve begins to flatten. The latest point, 145.1 crore, is a World Bank estimate based on census and survey data. The population tripled over 64 years, but the pace of growth has changed dramatically. The fastest rates were seen decades ago; now the line is bending toward a slower climb.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The headline count and the shape of how it got here.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the y-axis for total people; the x-axis shows the year.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume steady growth; the curve steepens then flattens, reflecting changing growth rates.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep axis labels large and sparse; use a single line with clear markers for key years.

chartExplainers.title: Population pyramid, 2025
chartExplainers.takeaway: The pyramid shows a thick working-age bulge and a narrowing base, signaling the end of rapid population growth.
chartExplainers.detail: This pyramid uses a UN median projection for 2030 to show the age-sex structure. Each horizontal bar represents a five-year age group; the left side is male, the right is female. The thickest bars are in the 20-24 range, with 12.5 crore people. Above age 30, the pyramid gradually narrows. At the base, the under-5 group has only 11.1 crore people, much smaller than the groups above it. This shape is typical for a country that has passed its high-fertility phase and is beginning to age.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Who those people are, by age and sex.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Left bars are male, right bars are female; the vertical axis is age, and length shows population.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare bar lengths between sexes directly without noting the scale; the pyramid is symmetrical by design.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a full-width pyramid on desktop; on mobile, keep labels short and preserve left/right symmetry.

chartExplainers.title: Annual population growth rate
chartExplainers.takeaway: Annual growth has fallen from 2.4% in 1961 to 0.9% in 2024, though the population still adds about 1.3 crore people a year.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks the percentage change in population each year. The line peaked in 1961 at 2.4% and has declined almost continuously since. By 2024, it reached 0.9%. Even that seemingly small rate adds roughly 1.3 crore people per year because the base population is huge. The trend is not linear; there are bumps, but the overall direction is downward. A declining growth rate does not mean the population is shrinking—only that its expansion is slowing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How fast the population is still rising each year.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line shows percent change per year; a falling line means slower growth, not population decline.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A declining rate does not mean population decline; the number still adds millions.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Sparse ticks and a single line keep it clean on small screens.

chartExplainers.title: Births per woman
chartExplainers.takeaway: Fertility has dropped from 5.92 births per woman in 1960 to 1.96 in 2024, falling below the replacement level.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the total fertility rate, the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if current birth rates persisted. In 1960, the figure was 5.92. Over six decades, it has fallen steadily to 1.96 in 2024. A rate of 2.1 is considered the replacement level for a stable population. India has now slipped below that threshold, meaning each generation will be smaller than the last if rates stay constant. This decline is the main driver behind the slowdown in population growth.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The main driver behind the growth slowdown.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line shows the average number of children per woman over time.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Fertility can stabilize or rise; the trend is not guaranteed to continue downward forever.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A clean line with few markers keeps it readable on mobile.

chartExplainers.title: Age structure today
chartExplainers.takeaway: The largest share of the population is in the working ages, with a clear bulge in the teens and twenties.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart breaks the population into fine age bands for a single year, using the same UN projection data as the pyramid. It highlights the concentration of people in the 15-34 age range. The working-age pool is deep, which can boost economic output if enough jobs are available. The proportion of very young and very old is smaller, creating a temporary structure that economists call a demographic dividend. This snapshot is a moment in time; the bulge will move up the age ladder in the years ahead.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The population split into life stages, not just three buckets.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars show each age group's share; notice the bulge in the 15-34 range.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is one year's snapshot, not a prediction; the bulge will age.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars work well on phones if labels are concise.

chartExplainers.title: Median age
chartExplainers.takeaway: The median age is projected to rise from 21.19 in 2000 to 47.78 by 2100, reflecting a steadily aging population.
chartExplainers.detail: The median age splits the population into two equal halves. In 2000, half of India was younger than 21.19. By the end of this century, under the UN median scenario, half will be older than 47.78. The line shows a continuous upward trend, with the fastest rise expected after 2040. This shift is a direct consequence of lower birth rates and longer lives. A higher median age does not mean the population is old overall today, but it points to a future where the typical Indian is middle-aged.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The single number for how old the country is.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line tracks the median age over time; the steeper the line, the faster the aging.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A rising median age means the population is aging, but many young people still exist.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A simple line with a clear trend is easy to read on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: How India's age mix has shifted
chartExplainers.takeaway: The child share fell from 40.6% to 24.6%, the working-age share rose from 56.1% to 68.2%, and the older share grew from 3.3% to 7.1%.
chartExplainers.detail: This multi-line chart tracks the share of three age groups since 1960. The green line (children) started at 40.6% and has been falling steadily, ending at 24.6% in 2024. The working-age line moved in the opposite direction, from 56.1% to 68.2%. The older-share line has stayed low but is now ticking upward. The crossover point, where working-age share surpasses child share, happened decades ago. The working-age share is now near its peak, a window that will close as the older share accelerates.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The shift that opened India's demographic-dividend window.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Three lines: children (0-14), working age (15-64), older (65+).
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read too much into small wiggles; focus on the long-run trends.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Multi-line charts work on mobile if lines are distinct and labels are minimal.

chartExplainers.title: Life expectancy at birth
chartExplainers.takeaway: Life expectancy at birth has risen from 62.75 years in 2000 to a projected 73.63 by 2030, with women outliving men by 3.4 years.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the average number of years a newborn could expect to live if current death rates stayed the same. Both sexes combined reached 73.63 in the 2030 projection, up from 62.75 in 2000. Women continuously live longer: 75.41 versus 71.99 for men. The improvement reflects gains in child survival, disease control, and nutrition. Life expectancy at birth is not a guarantee for any individual; it is a summary of today’s mortality risks.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How long people now live, by sex.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines for both sexes, male, and female; note the persistent gap.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Life expectancy at birth is not a prediction for anyone alive today.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Three lines can work if color-coded and labeled clearly.

chartExplainers.title: Life expectancy at 60
chartExplainers.takeaway: A 60-year-old woman could expect 16.51 more years, and a man 14.76 years, based on 2021 data, with figures lower than pre-pandemic years.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks the remaining years a person can expect at age 60. In 2021, it was 16.51 years for women and 14.76 for men. Both figures had been rising before COVID-19: in 2020, the combined value was 17.8 years. The dip reflects pandemic-era mortality. Even so, these numbers highlight that many Indians now live well into their seventies and eighties. As life expectancy at older ages improves, the needs for pensions, healthcare, and social support will grow.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How many more years someone who reaches 60 can expect.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines for male, female, and both sexes; watch for the pandemic drop.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are averages; many live longer, some shorter.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the chart clean with only a few labeled years.

chartExplainers.title: Child mortality by age
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2023, 27.75 children per 1,000 died before age five, and 24.5 per 1,000 died before age one.
chartExplainers.detail: Two lines illustrate child survival. The under-five mortality rate was 27.75 per 1,000 live births in 2023. The infant mortality rate (death before age one) was 24.5 per 1,000. The gap between the two lines shows that most under-five deaths happen in the first year. Both rates have declined dramatically from earlier decades, but the numbers remain substantial. For every 1,000 babies born, roughly 24 do not survive to their first birthday. These figures are WHO estimates, not official Indian SRS statistics.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Child survival, split into deaths before five and before one.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines: under-five and infant; the gap between them highlights first-year vulnerability.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Rates are per 1,000 live births, not per total population.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Two lines can be differentiated by color; a clear title helps on small screens.

chartExplainers.title: Child dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: The number of children per 100 working-age adults has fallen from 59.22 in 2000 to a projected 32.4 by 2030.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks the child dependency ratio over time. It counts how many people aged 0-14 there are for every 100 people aged 15-64. In 2000, the ratio was 59.22. By 2030, it is expected to drop to 32.4. The decline reflects the falling birth rate. A lower ratio means fewer children to feed and educate for each working-age adult. Not every adult works, and not every child is a burden, but the ratio captures a broad demographic pressure that is easing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How many children each 100 working-age adults support.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart over time; a lower ratio means fewer children per working-age adult.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is a demographic ratio, not an economic support measure.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A single line with a clear downward trend is easy on mobile.

chartExplainers.title: Old-age dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: The old-age dependency ratio is projected to rise from 7.35 in 2000 to 12.4 by 2030, and will keep climbing.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart shows the number of people aged 65 and older per 100 working-age adults. In 2000, it was 7.35. The UN median projection for 2030 puts it at 12.4. This ratio will continue to rise as the large working-age cohort ages and life expectancy improves. A higher ratio signals more retired people relative to potential workers. It does not mean every older person is dependent; many work or have family support. But it points to a growing demand for pensions, healthcare, and elder care.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How many older adults each 100 working-age adults support.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart over time; a rising ratio means an aging population burden.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Not all older adults are dependent; many work or support themselves.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A simple upward-trending line works well on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: Population scenarios to 2030
chartExplainers.takeaway: By 2100, India’s population could range from 99.1 crore under low fertility to 219.7 crore under high fertility, with a median projection of 150.5 crore.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart illustrates several UN projection scenarios from 2020 to 2100. The median path reaches 150.5 crore. The high-fertility variant climbs to 219.7 crore, while the low-fertility one drops to 99.1 crore. The spread is wide because small differences in how many children women have compound over decades. Scenarios are not predictions; they are ‘what-if’ exercises that show the sensitivity of future population size to fertility choices today. The chart also includes variants like constant mortality and zero migration for additional context.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How much the near future depends on fertility assumptions.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Multiple lines show different scenario paths from 2020 to 2100.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The title says 'to 2030' but the lines extend to 2100; focus on the full projection range.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use distinct colors and a legend that stacks vertically on phones.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India's population reached 145.1 crore in 2024, having more than tripled since 1960, but the annual growth rate has now slowed to 0.9% as the fertility rate dropped below two births per woman.
requiredConcepts: The total population count is a headcount of all residents, estimated from censuses and surveys.
Population growth rate is the annual percentage change, capturing births minus deaths plus net migration.
The fertility rate is the average number of children born to a woman over her lifetime.
The population pyramid shows age and sex structure, revealing past demographic events.
Life expectancy at birth is the average years a newborn would live if mortality patterns stayed constant.
Dependency ratios measure the number of dependents (children or older adults) per 100 working-age adults.
All projections depend on assumptions about future fertility, mortality, and migration.

conceptsToExplain: A population pyramid visualizes age groups on the vertical axis and the size of each group by sex.
A pyramid with a wide base means many young people; a narrowing base means fewer children.
sectionPlan.caveat: The pyramid here uses UN median projection for 2030, not current year.

sectionPlan.heading: How fast is India’s population still growing each year?
sectionPlan.job: Show the decline in the annual growth rate from 2.4% in 1961 to 0.9% in 2024.
conceptsToExplain: Population growth rate reflects births, deaths, and migration.
A declining growth rate still means the population is getting larger, just more slowly.
sectionPlan.caveat: Growth rate can be negative if deaths consistently exceed births.

sectionPlan.heading: Why is the growth rate slowing? What has happened to the number of births per woman?
sectionPlan.job: Connect the growth slowdown to the fertility decline from 5.92 in 1960 to 1.96 in 2024.
conceptsToExplain: Fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have if current age-specific rates persisted.
A rate near 2.1 is often called 'replacement level' for a stable population.
sectionPlan.caveat: Fertility is just one driver; mortality and migration also affect growth.

sectionPlan.heading: What share of the population are children, working-age adults, and older people?
sectionPlan.job: Present the age structure split into 0–14, 15–64, and 65+ shares, showing the shift since 1960.
conceptsToExplain: Age structure is the distribution of population across broad age groups.
A high share of working-age population can boost economic growth (demographic dividend).
sectionPlan.caveat: Shares are percentages of total; a growing older share will change care needs.

sectionPlan.heading: How old is the typical Indian? What is the median age?
sectionPlan.job: Show the median age rising from 21.2 in 2000 to a projected 47.8 by 2100 under the median scenario.
lockedNumbersToUse: Median age of population (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2100)
Median age of population (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2000)
conceptsToExplain: Median age is the age that divides the population into two equal halves.
A rising median age indicates an aging population.
sectionPlan.caveat: The median age by 2100 depends heavily on fertility assumptions.

sectionPlan.heading: How has India’s age mix shifted over the decades?
sectionPlan.job: Show the long-run trend: children’s share falling from 40.6% to 24.6%, working-age rising, older share still low but growing.
conceptsToExplain: The demographic transition: from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates.
The window when working-age share peaks is a one-time opportunity.
sectionPlan.caveat: The shift is smooth over decades; sudden changes are rare.

sectionPlan.heading: How long can an Indian newborn expect to live today?
sectionPlan.job: Present life expectancy at birth, by sex: 73.6 years overall in 2030 projection.
lockedNumbersToUse: Life expectancy by sex at birth (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2030)
Life expectancy by sex at birth (Median, Male, Not applicable): value (2030)
Life expectancy by sex at birth (Median, Female, Not applicable): value (2030)
conceptsToExplain: Life expectancy at birth is a synthetic measure based on current mortality rates.
sectionPlan.caveat: It is an average; many people live longer, some shorter.

sectionPlan.heading: Once someone reaches age 60, how many more years can they expect?
sectionPlan.job: Show life expectancy at age 60: 16.5 years for women, 14.8 for men in 2021.
lockedNumbersToUse: Life expectancy at age 60 (WHOSIS_000015): NumericValue (2021) for female and male
conceptsToExplain: Life expectancy at older ages captures remaining years after surviving earlier risks.
sectionPlan.caveat: Data are from 2021, COVID-19 may have affected figures.

sectionPlan.heading: What are the chances of a child dying before age five or before their first birthday?
sectionPlan.job: Show under-five and infant mortality rates: 27.7 and 24.2 per 1,000 live births in 2023.
conceptsToExplain: Under-five mortality includes deaths from birth to age 5; infant mortality is death before age 1.
Both are proxies for child health and healthcare access.
sectionPlan.caveat: These are UN IGME estimates, not official Indian SRS figures.

sectionPlan.heading: How many children does each 100 working-age adults have to support?
sectionPlan.job: Show child dependency ratio: 32.4 per 100 working-age adults in 2030 projection.
lockedNumbersToUse: Child dependency ratio (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2030)
conceptsToExplain: Child dependency ratio is the number of 0–14 year-olds divided by the 15–64 population, times 100.
sectionPlan.caveat: All children are counted as dependents, but some older children may work or contribute.

sectionPlan.heading: And how many older adults does each 100 working-age adults support?
sectionPlan.job: Show old-age dependency ratio: 12.4 per 100 in 2030 projection.
lockedNumbersToUse: Old-age dependency ratio (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2030)
conceptsToExplain: Old-age dependency ratio is the number of people 65+ divided by 15–64, times 100.
sectionPlan.caveat: Not all 65+ are dependent, just as not all 15–64 are working; it is a demographic measure.

sectionPlan.heading: Where is India’s population headed by 2100? What do the scenarios tell us?
sectionPlan.job: Explain the UN projection scenarios: median 150.5 crore, high-fertility 219.7 crore, low-fertility 99.1 crore.
lockedNumbersToUse: Total population by sex (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2100)
Total population by sex (High-fertility, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2100)
Total population by sex (Low-fertility, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2100)
conceptsToExplain: Scenarios are not predictions; they are if-then exercises based on different fertility assumptions.
sectionPlan.caveat: The wide range (99 crore to 220 crore) shows uncertainty: small differences in the number of children per woman compound over decades.

Line shows the steady aging of the population.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A count of all people living in a country at a given time, pieced together from censuses, surveys, and birth and death records. It is not a real-time count; it is the best available figure.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The 145.1 crore figure is an estimate; the exact number is never known with certainty.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average number of children a woman would have if she experienced current age-specific birth rates throughout her childbearing years. Think of it as the average family size in a particular year.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Fertility falling below 2 means, on average, each generation is smaller than the one before—this is the main brake on population growth.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The age that splits a population into two equal halves: half are younger, half are older. It is like the middle person in a queue sorted by age.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India’s median age is still young (around 28 in 2024), but it is rising fast as births slow.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of people aged 0-14 (child dependency) or 65+ (old-age dependency) per 100 people aged 15-64. It gives a rough measure of how many dependents the working-age population supports.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: A falling child dependency ratio and a still-low old-age dependency ratio is the 'demographic dividend' window when fewer dependents can free up resources.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average number of years a newborn would live if the death rates at each age stayed the same throughout its life. It reflects today’s health conditions, not a prophecy.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Rising life expectancy means people are living longer, which is good but also increases the number of older people.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of babies who die before their first birthday, per 1,000 live births in a given year. It is a sensitive indicator of healthcare quality.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Infant mortality has fallen sharply, but about 24 out of every 1,000 babies still do not reach age one.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A calculation of what could happen in the future if certain trends continue. It is a 'what-if' exercise, not a forecast. Scenarios use different assumptions (e.g., high, medium, low fertility).
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The wide range of population scenarios for 2100 shows how sensitive the future is to how many children women have today.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A rate that counts events (like deaths) relative to every 1,000 babies born alive. It standardizes the risk so you can compare across time or places.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Mortality rates are expressed per 1,000 to make them easier to grasp than very small decimals.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The percentage by which the total population changes from one year to the next. It is the net result of births, deaths, and migration.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: A growth rate of 0.9% still means India added about 1.3 crore people in 2024.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
